items.title: VS Code Wrapped: GitHub Universe 2026
items.lede: When we gathered at GitHub Universe in October 2025, working with agents in VS Code was still relatively new. A year later, working with agents has become the new normal. A single developer can put several agents to work on different problems, keep coding while those tasks move forward, and check back in to review the results.
items.text:
On this page

When we gathered at GitHub Universe in October 2025, working with agents in VS Code was still relatively new. A year later, working with agents has become the new normal. A single developer can put several agents to work on different problems, keep coding while those tasks move forward, and check back in to review the results. Work can continue on another machine, in another app, or in the cloud after your laptop closes. The editor that helps you write code is also becoming the place where you coordinate much more of the work it takes to ship software.

Imagine handing off a feature to Copilot, while an agent using the Claude harness investigates a bug, then opening the running app in a browser that both you and the agent can see and control. Project instructions and tools give those agents the context to work, and the Agents window brings their progress and changes together for review.

When you hand a task to an agent, it shouldn't matter which app you're using to launch the task. When you switch to another tool, the task should continue running. Over the last releases, we've worked to make these connected, continuous experiences across VS Code and other Copilot apps become reality.

In this blog post, we're zooming into how far VS Code has come since the last Universe, and what you can do with it today.

Agents that keep working

Developers can hand off more of the work without handing over the decisions that matter. We built on our Language Server Protocol and Debug Adapter Protocol experience to create the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), which just went 1.0.

Just as a language server makes code completion and Go to Definition available to different editors, an Agent Host brings agent functionality into an independent process. It manages sessions and provides access to multiple harnesses, models, files, and terminals.

AHP lets clients connect to those sessions and stay in sync. Cloud sessions run on GitHub's infrastructure, so closing your laptop doesn't stop them. You can continue the same session in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Mobile, github.com, or Copilot CLI. And because the protocol is open, anyone can build a client that works with the same live sessions as VS Code.

Choosing your agent

The agent harness is what coordinates the agent loop and connects the language model to context and tools.
We combined our Local VS Code harness with the Copilot CLI harness to create the new Copilot harness, now the default for new sessions in both the editor and Agents window. Built on the Microsoft Copilot SDK developed by GitHub, it brings more consistent agent behavior across VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. This also means that you can reuse your agent customizations across different Copilot experiences without modifications.

You can also use the Claude and Codex harnesses in VS Code through the Agent Host. Each runs on its provider’s own agent harness, with its own runtime and capabilities. VS Code brings their sessions together in one place, where you can manage work across agents without requiring every agent to work the same way.

Choosing your model

Access to multiple models remains one of Copilot's pillars. The model picker lets you select from Copilot and bring your own key models. You can specify options like reasoning effort and context size to optimize the model configuration for the task.

As newer and more capable models become available, choosing the right model for the task is becoming more and more difficult. Maybe one model is not the best for each part of the task.
Copilot Fusion autonomously chooses one model or orchestrates a set of models to solve the task at hand. In the Agents Window, you can also use the Compare Models feature in Preview to run different models and harnesses on the same task, review results side by side, and combine the best ideas. Together, these options help you balance speed, cost, and quality.

Managing parallel work

The work we started with Agent HQ in VS Code has grown into the Agents Window, a dedicated space to manage agents across all your workspaces and environments.

items.title: The Copilot harness: Building on a shared foundation
items.lede: The Copilot harness, built on the Copilot SDK, is now the default for new agent sessions in VS Code. Our goal is to keep the capabilities you love from VS Code's original, editor-specific Local harness and add the benefits of a runtime shared across Copilot products.
items.text:
On this page

The Copilot harness, built on the Copilot SDK, is now the default for new agent sessions in VS Code. Our goal is to keep the capabilities you love from VS Code's original, editor-specific Local harness and add the benefits of a runtime shared across Copilot products. By sharing fixes and optimizations instead of repeating work on separate harnesses, we can deliver improvements faster and focus more on important bugs, workflow gaps, and new capabilities.

Over the last several months, we've progressively rolled out the Copilot harness as the default, while monitoring data and user feedback at every stage to improve the experience. The Local harness is now deprecated and remains available during a three-month transition period before removal in February 2027 (unless your organization restricts its use).

TL;DR

- Efficiency and reliability gains: We assess both aspects through everyday VS Code workflows and controlled evaluations:

- In one online Business/Enterprise rollout comparison, the group defaulting to the Copilot harness used 14.2% fewer tokens per active device than those on the Local harness, with 9.6% lower estimated processing cost.

- In offline side-by-side VS Code evaluations, the Copilot harness had fewer errors and interruptions during long coding tasks than the Local harness.

- On repeatable tasks with the same model, published benchmarks found comparable task completion with fewer tokens in most tested configurations versus model-provider harnesses. They evaluated Copilot CLI, which shares the runtime VS Code integrates through the Copilot SDK.

- Capabilities beyond the Local harness: The shared foundation enables features and protections beyond what the Local harness supports:

- Copilot Fusion for multi-model work.

- Copilot runtime-enforced enterprise permission and sandbox policies.

- Agent Host sessions remain active after their project window closes, while VS Code remains running.

- Your workflow and transition:

- For local projects, the Copilot harness still runs on your machine in VS Code.

- What we've shipped based on your feedback.

- What's in progress or may need your attention below.

Why one shared harness

An agent harness supplies context and tools, coordinates actions such as edits and tests, and returns results to the model.

We first built the Local harness for interactive coding before a shared Copilot harness was available. That work shaped how you review agent edits and use tools supplied by VS Code extensions and MCP servers. We continually refined the harness with model providers and your feedback.

The Copilot harness uses the Copilot SDK to combine VS Code's supported editor integrations with the runtime shared by Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and other Microsoft products. The runtime is included in VS Code and works with existing Copilot plans.

Fixes or optimizations to that shared runtime benefit VS Code and other Copilot clients. This provides a more consistent experience across clients, and leaves more engineering time for VS Code-specific features, fixes, and workflow improvements.

What the data shows

We expanded the rollout of the Copilot harness as the default over several months, starting internally, then across Copilot plans, VS Code Insiders and Stable, and editor and Agents-window workflows. At each step, we reviewed key metrics alongside your feedback, and then used those findings to improve the product and plan further experiments.

We combine online evaluations, which show how the harness performs as people really work in VS Code, with offline evaluations, which run realistic development tasks under repeatable conditions. These offline evaluations include VS Code-specific comparisons and shared-runtime benchmarks. We'll next look at what these measurements tell us about efficiency, reliability, and task outcomes, then turn to how your feedback has shaped the experience.

Real online workflows: the VS Code rollout

Efficiency and processing cost

Across the Stable Business and Enterprise rollout stages we analyzed, estimates consistently pointed toward lower processing cost per active device with the Copilot harness as the default.
